claims.text: Increasing aluminum content within the solubility limit promotes formation of a homogeneous, continuous alumina-rich surface layer.
A continuous alumina-rich surface layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
A continuous alumina-rich surface layer improves corrosion resistance in aqueous chloride environments.
Increasing aluminum content enhances lattice distortion in the alloy.
The aluminum-induced lattice distortion maintains or increases mechanical strength.
A lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film can be prepared by magnetron sputtering.
The initial AlTiVNb film is amorphous.
The initial alloy is a uniform, chemically disordered solid solution.
A higher aluminum fraction increases the chemical driving force for Al2O3 formation during high-temperature exposure.
A higher aluminum fraction promotes protective Al2O3 formation in corrosive aqueous environments.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the lower-aluminum baseline in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will exhibit less weight gain than the baseline during oxidation at 800–1400 °C.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will have mechanical strength comparable to or slightly greater than the baseline.
The aluminum-enriched alloy will remain lightweight while gaining oxidation resistance, corrosion resistance, and mechanical robustness.
Exceeding the aluminum solubility limit can produce brittle intermetallic phases or compositional inhomogeneities.
Brittle intermetallic phases or inhomogeneities produced by excessive aluminum can degrade mechanical or corrosion properties.

contradictions.description: The material is described both as amorphous and as a solid solution. A chemically disordered amorphous phase is possible, but calling it a solid solution without clarifying whether a crystalline solid solution is intended creates structural ambiguity.

Formation of brittle phases at excessive aluminum content is presented as a condition under which the hypothesis no longer applies, but decreased strength from brittle-phase emergence is also presented as a falsifying result. The same observation could therefore be treated either as exclusion from scope or as falsification.
